findings.claim: The mark scheme rewards candidates who present the functionalist case (Durkheim on social solidarity, Parsons on meritocracy) and then systematically challenge it using at least one other perspective
findings.truth: No mark scheme is quoted or published in the spec, so the lesson invents an examiner claim. The advice itself is sound and can be given in the site's own voice ('the strongest answers...').
findings.evidence: spec assessment section prints only timing, marks, AOs and question styles; house rule bans fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims

findings.claim: Francis identified two contrasting forms of gendered pupil behaviour - 'laddish' behaviour among boys ... and 'under-the-radar rebellion' among girls
findings.truth: Becky Francis is correctly the spec's named feminist for the patriarchal nature of schools, and 'laddish' behaviour is genuinely hers. The exact phrase 'under-the-radar rebellion' could not be tied to a Francis publication; Wikipedia's page on Francis lists her gender-and-achievement books but no such term. The claim is plausible but unsourced.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 names Becky Francis; WebFetch en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Becky_Francis - no mention of the phrase

findings.claim: The 2024 examiner report identified the hidden curriculum question as one of the lowest-scoring items.
findings.truth: A fabricated source. No 2024 examiner report is cited anywhere in the spec or the unit, and no such finding can be verified. The teaching point (pupils confuse the hidden curriculum with the timetable) stands on its own without an invented citation.
findings.evidence: spec contains no examiner-report material; house rule treats invented examiner claims as FIX

findings.claim: Becker (Outsiders, 1963) introduced the concept of master status
findings.truth: Everett Hughes coined 'master status' in 'Dilemmas and Contradictions of Status' (1945). Becker applied it to deviance in Outsiders (1963). Becker's association with the term is correct; the claim that he introduced it is not.
findings.evidence: Hughes, American Journal of Sociology, 1945 - settled attribution in the sociological literature

findings.claim: The gender gap in favour of girls has widened slightly since the 1990s.
findings.truth: The direction is unsupported. Department for Education key stage 4 series show the girls-boys gap has been broadly stable since the mid-1990s, narrowing slightly after the reduction of coursework in the 2010s reforms. The defensible statement is that the gap has persisted.
findings.evidence: DfE key stage 4 attainment series (gap of roughly 8-10 percentage points across the period); no source supports 'widened'

findings.claim: Describing these trends - not just the current snapshot - is what examiners reward at the higher mark bands.
findings.truth: Another invented examiner claim. The advice is right; the appeal to what examiners reward is not evidenced and must be put in the site's own voice.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: official statistics from the Department for Education are large-scale, covering all schools in England and Wales
findings.truth: The Department for Education covers England only. Education is devolved, so Welsh school and attainment statistics come from the Welsh Government, and inspection in Wales is by Estyn, not Ofsted. This matters for a Wales-designated qualification.
findings.evidence: gov.uk departmental remit - DfE responsibilities apply to England; education devolved to the Welsh Government

findings.claim: Halsey's Origins and Destinations research combined survey data with follow-up interviews, using triangulation to increase confidence in the conclusions. (Repeated in the model answer to practice question 2.)
findings.truth: Origins and Destinations (Halsey, Heath and Ridge, 1980) rests on the 1972 Oxford Mobility Study, a single large interview-administered survey of men in England and Wales. That is one method delivered by interview, not a triangulated mixed-method design. I could not confirm any qualitative follow-up strand, and Wikipedia's Halsey page does not describe the book. Options: (a) leave it, since the sentence is only an illustration of triangulation; (b) move the exemplar to Ball's Beachside Comprehensive, which the same lesson already describes as observation plus interviews and which the spec names; (c) drop the exemplar sentence. Recommended: (b).
findings.evidence: Origins and Destinations uses the 1972 Oxford Mobility Study survey; WebFetch en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._H._Halsey returned no methodology detail
findings.ruling: Triangulation exemplar moved from Halsey (single survey) to Ball's Beachside (observation + interviews) in content and the model answer.

findings.claim: The unit teaches a question ladder of 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and 12 marks with the labels Multiple Choice, Define, Identify and Describe, Describe, Discuss and Evaluate (all six lessons).
findings.truth: The spec does not print the question ladder, so these tariffs cannot be verified. Nothing in them contradicts the facts the spec does give: the paper runs 1 hour 45 minutes, carries 100 marks and is 50% of the qualification, with a mix of short-answer, structured and extended-response questions, AO1 40 / AO2 40 / AO3 20 overall, and at least 15% of marks for research methods. No lesson asserts a 20- or 25-mark question, SPaG marks or another board's paper names.
findings.evidence: spec summary of assessment and section 3.1

summary: Sociology is accurate on the content that matters: every named thinker matches the spec (Durkheim, Parsons, Bowles and Gintis, Becky Francis, Hargreaves, Ball, Willis, Halsey), and dates, studies, Acts and the 7% private-school figure all check out; all 30 knowledge-check keys are correct. The real fault is fabricated exam authority - an invented 2024 examiner report plus two 'the mark scheme rewards' claims - with one unsupported gender-gap trend, one misattributed origin for master status and one England-versus-Wales error in a model answer.
